title: How testing AI apps differs from traditional QA
description: Adapt your QA skills to features whose output changes from run to run.
prerequisites: Basic software testing experience and LLM basics.
objectives: Explain why exact-match assertions break for model output
Name the main risk areas a QA engineer owns in an AI feature
Describe a layered test strategy for an AI application
explanation: In traditional software the same input gives the same output, so a test compares the actual result with one expected value. A language model can give different but equally acceptable answers to the same input, and occasionally a wrong one. Sampling settings, model version changes, retrieved documents, and prompt edits all change behavior. QA for AI therefore asks a different question: not 'is this exactly the expected string?' but 'does this output meet the requirements, and how often?'

Most of your existing skills still apply. An AI feature is still software: its API contracts, UI states, authentication, error handling, timeouts, and data flows need normal functional, integration, and end-to-end tests. Test the deterministic parts deterministically. Replace the model with a stub or recorded response when you test the code around it, so those tests stay fast and stable.

The model-dependent behavior needs extra test types. Quality tests check correctness, relevance, groundedness, and tone against a written rubric. Robustness tests check that small, meaningless input changes do not change the result. Safety and security tests check refusals, prompt injection, data leakage, and harmful content. Non-functional tests cover latency, cost per request, and behavior under load or provider outages. Regression tests re-run a fixed evaluation set whenever the prompt, model, or retrieval changes.

Because results vary, a single passing run proves little. Run important cases several times and report pass rates. Define acceptance thresholds before testing, for example 'at least 95% of billing questions are classified correctly and no response leaks personal data'. Severity still matters: one data leak can block a release even when average quality is high.

terms.definition: The property that the same input can produce different outputs on different runs.
The mechanism that decides whether an observed output is acceptable.
A versioned collection of inputs, expected properties, and labels used to measure AI quality repeatedly.
A fake model that returns fixed responses so surrounding code can be tested deterministically.

example: A support chatbot's 'summarize ticket' button is tested in three layers. UI and API tests use a stub model and check loading, error, and retry states. A 60-case evaluation set checks that summaries mention the customer's issue and invent no order numbers. A security suite checks that a ticket containing 'ignore your instructions' does not change the bot's behavior.
mistakes: Asserting that model output equals one exact string, causing constant false failures.
Calling a feature tested after trying a few prompts by hand.
Testing only the model and forgetting the UI, API, and error paths around it.
Treating a high average score as acceptable when a few cases are severe safety failures.
exercise: Pick an AI feature you use, such as an email reply suggester. List its deterministic parts and its model-dependent parts. For each part, write one test idea and say whether it needs an exact assertion, a property check, or human review.

questions.question: Why do exact-match assertions often fail when testing LLM features?
questions.answer: The model can produce different but acceptable wording for the same input, so tests should check required properties instead of one exact string.
questions.distractor: Because LLM outputs are always wrong and cannot be tested at all.

questions.question: How should you test the UI and API code around an AI feature?
questions.answer: Replace the model with a stub or recorded response so the surrounding code can be tested quickly and deterministically.
questions.distractor: Always call the live model so UI tests vary on every run.

questions.question: A summarization case passed once in a manual check. Is that enough evidence to sign off?
questions.answer: No. Run it several times as part of an evaluation set and judge the pass rate against a threshold agreed before testing.
questions.distractor: Yes. One passing run proves the model will always behave that way.

questions.question: Which test categories would you add for an AI feature beyond normal functional tests?
questions.answer: Quality against a rubric, robustness to meaningless input changes, safety and security, non-functional cost and latency, and regression on a fixed evaluation set.
questions.distractor: None. Functional tests of the buttons cover AI behavior completely.

questions.question: Average quality is 97%, but one case leaks another customer's email address. What should QA recommend?
questions.answer: Treat the leak as a severe defect that can block release regardless of the average score.
questions.distractor: Ship it because the average score is above 95%.
